name: Function Word Profiling
description: Analyzes the subconscious distribution of function words (articles, prepositions, conjunctions, pronouns) which act as a unique, uncontrollable biometric fingerprint for authorial identity.
algorithm: Closed-Class Lexical Distribution & Burrows's Delta Analysis
mechanism: While content words (nouns, verbs, adjectives) dictate *what* a text is about, function words (the, of, and, in, a) dictate *how* it is cognitively structured. Function words constitute nearly 50% of the English language, yet humans use them almost entirely subconsciously. Decades of computational stylometry (authorship attribution) have proven that every human has a unique, highly stable mathematical fingerprint based on the frequencies and ratios of these 'invisible' words. AI models, however, are an amalgamation of billions of authors. Rather than possessing a singular, stable human fingerprint, an LLM outputs an overwhelmingly generic, perfectly averaged 'statistical ghost' distribution. This method utilizes Burrows's Delta metric to measure the relative frequencies of over 300 closed-class function words against an immense corpus of baseline human writing. If the function word distribution achieves a near-perfect 'vanilla' statistical mean—lacking the idiosyncratic, slightly asymmetrical function word ratios that organically occur even in professional human writing—the text is flagged as a machine-generated synthesis.
useCase: The gold standard for forensic authorship attribution, ideal for scrutinizing highly formal or academic documents where other stylistic quirks (like slang or emotion) are already suppressed.
strengths:
• Virtually impossible for a human (or an AI prompting a persona) to consciously manipulate, as function word selection occurs below the threshold of conscious thought.
• Highly resilient across different genres and topics; a writer's function word fingerprint remains stable whether they are writing a technical manual or a love letter.
• Backed by over three decades of peer-reviewed, court-admissible forensic linguistics research.
limitations:
• Requires a substantial text length (typically >300 words) to establish a statistically significant distribution curve.
• Cannot easily differentiate between different LLMs (e.g., Claude vs. GPT-4), as all heavily-aligned models converge toward similar 'averaged' linguistic centroids.
• Heavily reliant on language-specific, closed-class dictionaries, requiring entirely separate mathematical models for English, Spanish, Japanese, etc.
parameters:
Analysis: 300+ Closed-Class Word Extraction & Z-Score Normalization
Metric: Burrows's Delta Stylistic Divergence vs Human Centroid
Output: 0-100 Stylometric Homogenization (Algorithmic Averaging) Score
accuracy: High — 80-88% on multi-paragraph text. It is one of the most reliable and academically verified methods for distinguishing organic human cognition from statistical text generation.

references.title: Burrows, J. F. (2002). Delta: A Measure of Stylistic Difference and Its Literary History. Literary and Linguistic Computing.
Kestemont, M. (2014). Function Words in Authorship Attribution: From Black Magic to Theory? EACL.
